listening.title: Queen's University students blast off to US for Nasa robotics competition
listening.topic: A team of engineering students from Queen's University Belfast is competing in NASA's Lunabotics competition in Florida, where they will test a robot designed to perform tasks on the Moon.
listening.topic_zh: 來自貝爾法斯特女王大學的工程學生團隊將前往佛羅里達參加NASA的月球機器人競賽，測試他們設計的月球任務機器人。
listening.transcript_excerpt: Space exploration has long captured the human imagination, but today it is increasingly young engineers who are turning those dreams into reality. A team of ten students from Queen's University Belfast is preparing to travel to Florida to compete in NASA's prestigious Lunabotics competition. This university-level event challenges teams to design, build, and operate a robot capable of performing tasks that would be required on a real lunar mission. The Queen's University team built their robot entirely in a university laboratory, and their machine must be capable of digging up lunar material, navigating over obstacles, and using that excavated material to construct a wall — a task that mirrors genuine challenges faced during moon surface operations. The team is divided into three specialist groups: software, electronics, and mechanical engineering. Jamie Smith, the software team lead and a third-year electrical engineering student, explained that one of their biggest challenges was developing autonomous capabilities for the rover, meaning the robot must make certain decisions independently. To validate their software before the physical robot was ready, the team built detailed computer simulations of the rover's behaviour. Meanwhile, PhD student Jack Fitzpatrick leads the mechanical team, ensuring the robot's physical structure can withstand the demanding conditions of the competition. Having already won a qualifying round earlier this year, the team now faces international competition from universities across Australia, India, and the United States at the University of Central Florida. For these students, the competition represents far more than an academic exercise — it is a genuine step towards the future of space exploration.

vocabulary.definition: capable of operating independently without direct human control, especially referring to machines or systems that can make their own decisions
vocabulary.definition_zh: 自主的；能在無人直接控制下獨立運作的
vocabulary.example: The team programmed the rover to have autonomous capabilities so it could navigate obstacles without human input.

vocabulary.definition: NASA's university-level robotics competition in which student teams design and build robots intended to perform excavation and construction tasks on the lunar surface
vocabulary.definition_zh: 月球機器人競賽；NASA舉辦的大學級機器人設計與操作競賽，模擬月球表面任務
vocabulary.example: Winning the regional qualifying round gave the Queen's University team a place in the international Lunabotics finals in Florida.

vocabulary.definition: the process of digging into the ground or a surface to remove material, often used in engineering, archaeology, or construction contexts
vocabulary.definition_zh: 挖掘；從地面或表面移除物料的過程
vocabulary.example: The robot's primary function was the excavation of lunar regolith, which could then be used to build protective structures.

vocabulary.definition: a computer-generated model or representation of a real-world process, used to test systems or predict outcomes before physical implementation
vocabulary.definition_zh: 模擬；以電腦模型重現真實過程，用於在實際執行前測試系統
vocabulary.example: The software team ran hundreds of simulations to ensure the rover would respond correctly in various terrain conditions.

vocabulary.definition: a structured, interdisciplinary methodology used to design and manage complex systems throughout their life cycle, ensuring all components work together effectively
vocabulary.definition_zh: 系統工程流程；一種跨學科的結構化方法，用於設計和管理複雜系統，確保各組件協同運作
vocabulary.example: NASA requires all Lunabotics teams to follow the systems engineering process when designing and documenting their lunar robots.

questions.q: What are the robots in the Lunabotics competition required to do?
options: A: Fly to the Moon and collect samples remotely
B: Dig up lunar material, navigate obstacles, and build a wall
C: Repair existing lunar equipment and return to base
D: Photograph the lunar surface and transmit data to Earth
questions.explanation: The article explicitly states that robots must dig up lunar material, drive over obstacles, and use the material to form a wall, making B the correct answer.

questions.q: Why did the software team build rover simulations before the physical robot was complete?
options: A: Because the competition required simulation results to be submitted in advance
B: To demonstrate the robot's capabilities to NASA judges online
C: To test their software before they actually had a physical rover to work with
D: Because physical testing was prohibited under competition rules
questions.explanation: Jamie Smith explained that the team had to build rover simulations to test their software before they actually had a physical robot, confirming C as the correct answer.

questions.q: How did the Queen's University team qualify for the international competition in Florida?
options: A: They were directly invited by NASA based on their academic results
B: They submitted a design proposal that was selected by an international panel
C: They won a qualifying round of the competition earlier in the year
D: They were chosen as the sole representative team from the United Kingdom
questions.explanation: The article states the team made it to the competition following their win at the competition earlier this year, making C the correct answer.

reading.title: Student-Led Space Robotics: Engineering the Future of Lunar Exploration
reading.passage:
The emergence of student-led robotics competitions as a pipeline for developing space engineering talent represents one of the most significant shifts in how space agencies are cultivating the next generation of scientists and engineers. NASA's Lunabotics competition exemplifies this trend, challenging university teams worldwide to apply professional systems engineering methodologies to the design, construction, and operation of robots intended for lunar deployment.

The competition is structured around authentic engineering challenges that mirror those faced by professional aerospace teams. Participating robots must demonstrate the capacity to excavate lunar regolith — the loose material covering the Moon's surface — traverse uneven terrain, and utilise the excavated material for construction purposes such as building protective barriers. These tasks are not merely academic exercises; they reflect genuine priorities in NASA's Artemis programme, which aims to establish a sustainable human presence on the Moon within this decade.

A team of ten students from Queen's University Belfast recently qualified for the international finals of this competition, scheduled to take place at the University of Central Florida. The team's interdisciplinary composition — divided into software, electronics, and mechanical engineering sub-groups — reflects the collaborative nature of real-world space missions. Notably, the software team faced the considerable challenge of developing autonomous navigation capabilities for their rover, requiring the creation of sophisticated computer simulations to validate their algorithms prior to having access to a physical prototype.

The educational value of such competitions extends far beyond technical skill acquisition. Students are immersed in project management, cross-disciplinary communication, and iterative problem-solving — competencies that are increasingly valued across all engineering sectors. For institutions such as Queen's University Belfast, participation at this level also enhances global academic visibility and strengthens research partnerships with leading space organisations. The broader implication is clear: student robotics competitions are no longer peripheral activities but are becoming central to the development of credible, mission-ready aerospace engineers.

questions.statement: NASA's Lunabotics competition requires teams to follow a professional systems engineering methodology when designing their robots.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly states that the competition challenges teams to 'apply professional systems engineering methodologies to the design, construction, and operation of robots,' confirming this statement is True.

questions.statement: The Queen's University Belfast team consists of students from more than three different engineering disciplines.
questions.explanation: The passage states the team is divided into three sub-groups — software, electronics, and mechanical engineering — indicating exactly three disciplines, not more than three, making this statement False.

questions.statement: NASA's Artemis programme intends to send robotic missions to Mars before returning humans to the Moon.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions the Artemis programme aims to establish a human presence on the Moon but provides no information about Mars missions. This cannot be confirmed or denied from the passage alone.

questions.q: According to the passage, what was a significant challenge faced specifically by the software sub-team?
options: A: Securing funding to purchase the physical components of the rover
B: Communicating technical requirements to the mechanical engineering group
C: Developing autonomous navigation capabilities and testing them via simulation before a prototype existed
D: Meeting the competition's deadline for submitting the systems engineering documentation
questions.explanation: The passage clearly states that the software team faced 'the considerable challenge of developing autonomous navigation capabilities for their rover, requiring the creation of sophisticated computer simulations to validate their algorithms prior to having access to a physical prototype,' making C the correct answer.

speaking.topic: Describe a time when you worked as part of a team to complete a challenging project or task.
speaking.topic_zh: 描述一次你與團隊合作完成一項具有挑戰性的專案或任務的經歷。

part2.cue_card:
Describe a time when you worked as part of a team to complete a challenging project or task.

You should say:
• What the project or task was
• Who was involved in the team and what roles people played
• What challenges you faced during the process
• And explain what you learned from the experience and whether the team was successful.
band_tips: Use a range of narrative tenses accurately — past simple for completed actions, past continuous for background context, and past perfect to show what had happened before key moments, to demonstrate grammatical range to the examiner.

Incorporate topic-specific and abstract vocabulary naturally, such as 'interdisciplinary collaboration,' 'iterative problem-solving,' 'autonomous decision-making,' and 'optimise performance,' rather than relying on basic words like 'good' or 'difficult.'

Structure your response with a clear introduction, chronological development of the story, and a reflective conclusion about what you gained — this demonstrates coherence and shows the examiner you can organise extended speech effectively.

part3.q: Do you think universities should prioritise practical, project-based learning over traditional lectures and examinations?
part3.q_zh: 你認為大學應該優先推行以實踐和專案為基礎的學習，而非傳統的講課與考試模式嗎？
key_points: Project-based learning develops transferable skills such as teamwork, time management, and real-world problem-solving that examinations alone cannot assess effectively.
However, theoretical foundations established through lectures remain essential — without a solid academic grounding, students may struggle to apply practical skills in novel or complex situations.
A balanced, hybrid curriculum that integrates both approaches is likely to produce the most well-rounded graduates who are prepared for both professional environments and further academic research.

part3.q: To what extent do you believe international competitions like NASA's Lunabotics benefit the countries whose students participate?
part3.q_zh: 你認為像NASA月球機器人競賽這類國際競賽，對參賽學生所屬的國家有多大益處？
key_points: Such competitions elevate a nation's profile in the global STEM community and can attract international research investment and collaborative partnerships to participating universities.

Students who gain high-level exposure to cutting-edge engineering challenges are more likely to return to their home countries and contribute to domestic innovation ecosystems and technology industries.

There is also a significant soft-power dimension — national participation in prestigious international competitions signals scientific credibility and can influence diplomatic and academic relationships.

part3.q: Some people argue that space exploration is a waste of resources that should be directed towards solving problems on Earth. How far do you agree with this view?
part3.q_zh: 有些人認為太空探索是浪費資源，這些資源應該用於解決地球上的問題。你在多大程度上同意這一觀點？
key_points: This argument has considerable merit — acute global challenges such as climate change, poverty, and disease arguably demand more immediate financial investment than missions to the Moon or Mars.

Nevertheless, space research has historically generated transformative technologies with direct earthly applications, including GPS, water purification systems, and medical imaging technologies, demonstrating that the two goals are not mutually exclusive.

The framing of the question as an either-or choice may itself be misleading — governments and private entities can simultaneously invest in both space exploration and social welfare programmes, and the economic returns from space technology often justify the expenditure.

part3.q: How important is it for young people to develop skills in robotics and artificial intelligence, and what role should governments play in this?
part3.q_zh: 年輕人學習機器人技術和人工智能技能有多重要？政府在其中應扮演什麼角色？
key_points: As automation increasingly reshapes the global labour market, proficiency in robotics and AI is transitioning from a specialist advantage to a near-essential competency for career resilience across multiple sectors.

Governments have a responsibility to ensure equitable access to STEM education — without strategic policy intervention, advanced technical skills risk becoming concentrated among already-privileged demographics, exacerbating existing social inequalities.

Beyond school curricula, governments can incentivise industry partnerships, fund national competitions modelled on events like Lunabotics, and establish mentorship programmes that connect young people with practicing engineers and scientists.

writing.task2_question: In recent years, governments and private organisations have significantly increased investment in space exploration and robotics technology. Some people believe this investment is essential for the future of humanity, while others argue that these resources would be better spent addressing urgent problems on Earth such as poverty and climate change. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
writing.task2_question_zh: 近年來，政府和私人機構大幅增加對太空探索和機器人技術的投資。有些人認為這對人類的未來至關重要，而另一些人則認為這些資源最好用於解決地球上的緊迫問題，如貧困和氣候變化。討論兩種觀點並給出你自己的意見。

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use at the start of a body paragraph to introduce a perspective that has broad, general support before you develop or challenge it
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於段落開頭，引出一個廣為認可的觀點，然後進一步發展或反駁
useful_phrases.example: It is widely acknowledged that investment in robotics and space technology can yield significant long-term economic and scientific benefits for society as a whole.

useful_phrases.phrase: proponents of this view contend that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when presenting the argument of one side in a discussion essay, particularly to signal that you are fairly representing a position before offering balance
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於呈現某一方的論點，特別是在討論型作文中公正陳述立場後作出平衡
useful_phrases.example: Proponents of this view contend that the technologies developed through space research have historically found critical applications in everyday life on Earth.

useful_phrases.phrase: this argument, while superficially compelling, overlooks the fact that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when transitioning to a counter-argument or refutation, allowing you to acknowledge the opposing view's appeal before dismantling it
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於轉換至反駁觀點時，先承認對方論點的表面合理性，再提出反駁
useful_phrases.example: This argument, while superficially compelling, overlooks the fact that space research and social investment are not mutually exclusive policy priorities.

useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use when shifting focus from immediate concerns to broader, future-oriented consequences of a policy or trend, which demonstrates sophisticated analytical thinking
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於將討論焦點從眼前問題轉向某項政策或趨勢的長遠影響，展示深層分析思維
useful_phrases.example: The long-term implications of neglecting STEM education and space research investment could be a significant decline in national competitiveness and technological capacity.

useful_phrases.phrase: on balance, it would appear that
useful_phrases.when_to_use: Use in the conclusion or at the end of a body paragraph to signal a measured, considered judgement after weighing both sides of an argument
useful_phrases.when_to_use_zh: 用於結論或段落末尾，表示在權衡雙方論點後作出審慎、平衡的判斷
useful_phrases.example: On balance, it would appear that a diversified approach to public investment — one that funds both space exploration and domestic social programmes — represents the most rational and equitable policy direction.

outline.intro: Begin by contextualising the rapid growth of investment in space technology and robotics, then clearly identify the tension between its perceived long-term value and the urgency of present-day global challenges. End with a thesis statement that signals you will discuss both perspectives before presenting your own reasoned position.
outline.body1: Present the case in favour of prioritising space exploration and robotics investment. Argue that such investment generates breakthrough technologies with wide-ranging earthly applications, creates high-skilled employment, and prepares humanity for long-term survival challenges such as resource depletion. Use the example of student competitions like NASA's Lunabotics as evidence that these investments also cultivate future scientific talent.
outline.body2: Present the counter-argument that immediate human crises — including extreme poverty, inadequate healthcare, and accelerating climate change — demand urgent and proportionally greater resource allocation. Acknowledge that the benefits of space technology, while real, are often long-delayed and unevenly distributed, and that vulnerable populations cannot afford to wait for those returns.
outline.conclusion: Offer a balanced personal opinion that rejects the false binary between space investment and social investment. Argue that well-governed economies can pursue both, and that the educational and technological spillovers from space robotics research — exemplified by teams like Queen's University Belfast — ultimately serve broader human development goals. Close with a forward-looking statement about the role of the next generation of engineers.
